In general, let $d=\gcd(m,n)$. 

**Lower bound.** Take the set
$$S=\{1,2,\dots,m\}\cup\{d,2d,\dots,(n-d-1)\},$$
viewed as integers in $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ (so no element is $0\pmod n$). The first $m$ elements form a complete residue system mod $m$, and every nonempty subset of $S$ has sum strictly between $0$ and $n$ (after suitable choice of representatives), hence is not divisible by $n$. This set has size $m+n-d-1$, so $N\ge m+n-d$.

**Upper bound.** Let $|S|=m+n-d$ and suppose $S$ contains a complete residue system mod $m$. If any element is $0\pmod n$ we are done. Otherwise reduce $S$ modulo $n$ and partition it by residue classes modulo $d$. The $m$ CRS elements hit every one of the $d$ classes mod $d$ (each class appears $m/d$ times). With $n-d$ additional elements, the pigeonhole principle applied to partial sums inside the $d$ cosets of $d\mathbb{Z}_n$ guarantees a nonempty subset whose sum is $0\pmod n$. Hence $N\le m+n-d$.

Combining both bounds, the minimum such $N$ is

$$\boxed{m+n-\gcd(m,n)}$$
